# Incident Report — MTA 2024-08-15 Traffic Analysis Exercise

## 1. Victim Host

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 address | 10.8.15.133 |
| MAC address | 00:1c:bf:03:54:82 (Intel) |
| Windows hostname | DESKTOP-H8ALZBV |
| AD domain | lafontainebleu.org |
| Logged-in user | plucero (confirmed via Kerberos AS-REQ CNameString) |

Identity grounded in DHCP requests (hostname option), NBNS name registration, and Kerberos traffic all correlating to 10.8.15.133 / 00:1c:bf:03:54:82. Gateway: 00:16:9c:02:a7:4b (10.8.15.1). No other internal host on the /24 generated traffic besides the DHCP/DNS server (10.8.15.4).

## 2. Malware Family

**Attribution: BEHAVIORAL, not signature-confirmed.** No IDS/Suricata alert file was present in the evidence directory, and no AV/YARA scan was run — this identification rests entirely on observed network TTPs.

The chain matches a **JS-downloader-delivered loader/RAT infection** (fake-shipping-invoice lure → obfuscated JScript downloader → BITS-fetched PE loader → encrypted HTTP beaconing). Distinctive fingerprints observed:
- Obfuscated `.js` dropper padded with ~7 MB of unrelated document text (MPI spec, IPCC reports, PIAAC survey text) to inflate file size and evade sandboxing — a known loader-family evasion technique.
- Malicious payload downloaded via abused **Windows BITS service** (`User-Agent: Microsoft BITS/7.8`) directly from a raw IP rather than a legitimate CDN — MITRE T1197.
- Resulting C2 beaconing uses a **corrupted/spaced User-Agent** string (`Mozilla / 5.0 (compatible; MSIE 6.0; Windows NT 5.1; SV1; .NET CLR 1.0.3705)`) that does not match the real host (Windows 10/11, Edge 127) — a hardcoded, non-genuine UA typical of commodity RAT/stealer HTTP C2 (e.g., Remcos-style beaconing), plus a large base64 blob carried in the `Cookie` header (encrypted bot ID) and encrypted binary POST bodies.
- No family name string, mutex, or config was recoverable from the downloaded binary itself (imports limited to KERNEL32/ADVAPI32/SHELL32/ole32/WS2_32; internal name `release.dll`), so I am **not** asserting a specific named family with high confidence — treat as "loader + HTTP-based backdoor/stealer, family unconfirmed."

## 3. Timeline (capture-relative, local time UTC+4 per pcap)

| Time | Event |
|---|---|
| 04:10:55 | First DNS query for `quote.checkfedexexp.com` |
| 04:10:58 | GET to `quote.checkfedexexp.com/managements?...` from real Edge/127 browser → downloads ZIP (`Invoice 876597035_003.zip`, served via Cloudflare, `Content-Type: application/octet-stream`) |
| 04:11:24 | HTTPS connection to `business.checkfedexexp.com` (172.67.170.159:443) |
| 04:11:59 | BITS (`Microsoft BITS/7.8`) HEAD/GET to `72.5.43.29/data/0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4` → 159,232-byte PE32+ DLL delivered |
| 04:13:00 – 04:42:25 | 308 short-lived HTTP GET/POST connections to `72.5.43.29:80`, ~every 6 seconds — C2 beaconing, runs to end of capture |

## 4. Indicators of Compromise

**C2 / infrastructure**
- `72.5.43.29:80` — primary C2 endpoint (payload host + beaconing target, 308 sessions observed)
- `104.21.55.70:80` / `172.67.170.159:80,443` — Cloudflare anycast IPs fronting the malicious domains below

**Malicious domains**
- `quote.checkfedexexp.com` — fake FedEx invoice/delivery lure, served the initial ZIP payload
- `business.checkfedexexp.com` — same actor infrastructure, contacted over TLS shortly after initial infection; also referenced in cleartext inside the JS dropper (`https://business.checkfedexexp.com/data-privacy?zj=ZzqRKxVRQ&pOd=GEokiOXFwH&sourcedp=tQMQJlIo&Tfocontent`)

**Malicious URLs**
- `http://quote.checkfedexexp.com/managements?16553a25e45250a41fd5&endeds=MIGpq&JStx=59bf050d37df88a9-ade43358-eaa1220b-0571422b-0f33e6aa150e86bafd0ed4&Ld=9d7502d88d752a27b1d00587309184b5a215` — initial ZIP delivery
- `http://72.5.43.29/data/0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4` — DLL payload download (via BITS)
- `http://72.5.43.29/` — repeated GET/POST C2 beacon endpoint

**Transferred files / hashes**
| File | Type | Size | SHA256 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Invoice 876597035_003.zip` | ZIP (delivered w/ Content-Disposition) | 2,767,804 bytes | 798563fcf7600f7ef1a35996291a9dfb5f9902733404dd499e2e736ea1dc6fc5 |
| `Invoice-876597035-003-8331775-8334138.js` | Obfuscated JScript downloader (inside ZIP) | 6,990,020 bytes | dab98819d1d7677a60f5d06be210d45b74ae5fd8cf0c24ec1b3766e25ce6dc2c |
| `0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4` | PE32+ DLL (x64), fetched via BITS from 72.5.43.29 | 159,232 bytes | b7aec5f73d2a6bbd8cd920edb4760e2edadc98c3a45bf4fa994d47ca9cbd02f6 |

## 5. Notes on evidence hygiene
An earlier `tshark --export-objects` run wrote into a `/tmp` directory that already contained stale exports from an unrelated prior session (files named `TeamViewer`, `am_delta_patch_*.exe`, dated across three different days). Those were **not** re-verified against this pcap's HTTP request list and are excluded from this report — all IOCs above were re-extracted into a clean directory and confirmed against this specific capture's traffic.
